text: Place n queens on an n by n chessboard so that no two queens attack each other. Return all distinct solutions, in any order. Each solution is a board, with Q for a queen and a dot for an empty square.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Just to make sure I'm understanding this correctly — two queens attack if they share a row, a column, or a diagonal, in either direction. And I need every full board, not just the count. Is that right?
Yes. Every board, as a list of strings.
Got it. Are there any constraints on the input size?
n is between one and nine.

OK. Nine is tiny, so an exponential search is fine. The real cost is the size of the output. Let me run through the examples. n equals four gives two boards, and one is the mirror of the other. n equals one gives a single board with one queen. And I know n equals two and three have no solutions, so the answer can be an empty list.

Hmm, let me think about this for a sec. A naive approach would be to try every way to put n queens on n squared squares, then check each board. That's way too many. The first big cut: two queens can't share a row, so each row has exactly one queen. This problem reminds me of generating permutations by backtracking: row r picks a column, and no column repeats. So it's one recursion level per row, try each column, and prune the moment a queen is attacked.

Here's the plan. One: level r places the queen for row r; when r reaches n, save a copy of the board. Two: skip a column if its column, slash diagonal, or backslash diagonal is taken. Three: place, set the three flags, recurse, then clear the flags and remove the queen. One thing worth flagging — since the row is the recursion level, I only need flags for columns and the two diagonals, each checked in constant time. On a slash diagonal, r plus c is constant. On a backslash diagonal, r minus c is constant, but it can be negative, so I shift it by n minus one. Both kinds have two n minus one diagonals. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?

Alright, let me code this up. The main function builds an all-dot board, the flag arrays, and starts the search at row zero. The search saves the board when every row is filled; otherwise it tries each column, skips a blocked one, and does place, recurse, undo. The undo is the exact mirror of the do: the same four flags go back to false, and the square goes back to a dot. Pushing the board into the answer copies it, so later changes don't touch saved answers.
I see you set row of r. Where do you read it?

Good catch — I don't. The row array is written in two lines and never read. Level r always places exactly one queen in row r, so a row can never clash. That's the same point I made in the plan; the array is left over. Removing it gives byte-identical output for n from one to twelve, and no time difference. I'd delete it.

Let's dry-run the code with an example. n equals four, expected two boards. The row that matters is the first branch: with a queen at zero, zero, row one tries column two and row two is dead at once; column three gets one row further, then dies too. So the whole branch is undone back to row zero. Starting from columns one and two, each branch finds one solution; column three dies again. Seventeen calls, sixteen placements, two solutions, in the expected order. Let's also test with corner cases. n equals one: one board, two calls. n equals two and three: an empty list. The counts for n from one to nine — one, zero, zero, two, ten, four, forty, ninety-two, three fifty-two — match a brute force.
Which bugs would be easy to make here?

One thing worth flagging — the scary ones here are the silent ones. Forget the plus n minus one: the backslash index can go negative. In a normal build the output is still correct, so tests pass; only the address sanitizer catches it. Size the diagonal arrays n instead of two n minus one: even quieter. A vector of bool packs bits, so the extra indices stay inside one sixty-four-bit word, and even the sanitizer says nothing. Still undefined behavior. Forget to put the dot back: the flags are still reset, so the counts are all correct, but the boards have extra queens left over. A test that only checks the count misses it. Forget to reset the flags: that one is loud — n equals four returns zero boards.

Let me think about complexity here. The time complexity is n factorial placements as an upper bound: row zero has n choices, row one at most n minus one free columns, and so on. The diagonals cut far more: about two thousand placements at n equals eight, and about eighty-four hundred at n equals nine, around half a millisecond. On top of that, each solution costs n squared to copy the board. The space complexity is O of n for the recursion depth and the flags, plus n squared for the working board. The output itself is the number of solutions times n squared.
What if I only want the number of solutions?

I'd drop the board completely; the flags alone decide everything, and the base case just counts. Then I'd make it faster with bitmasks: the three flag arrays become three ints. The free columns for this row are one expression, I take the lowest free bit each time, and the diagonal masks shift by one each row, because a diagonal moves one column per row. I only visit free columns, so there's no skipping at all. One more trick: symmetry. A board and its mirror are both solutions, so I only try row-zero columns in the left half, double the count, and handle the middle column on its own when n is odd. That's about half the work.

Nicely done. Three things stood out. You used one queen per row to drop the row check, and you owned it right away when I pointed at the unused row array. You explained the diagonal indexing, including why r minus c needs the n minus one shift and why both arrays are two n minus one. And you knew which bugs stay silent: a negative index that only the sanitizer sees, and a missing board reset that count-only tests miss. Good work.
